body:
The 10th Sikh Guru

Guru Gobind Singh (1666–1708) was the 10th and last human Sikh Guru. He succeeded Guru Tegh Bahadur after the latter's death in 1675. Guru Gobind Singh is especially associated with 2 major developments: the formation of the Khalsa in 1699 and the recognition of the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru in 1708.

Why was the Khalsa formed?

By the late 17th century, the Sikh community had experienced growing political pressure and conflict. The execution of Guru Arjan in 1606 and the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur in 1675 formed part of this historical background.

Guru Gobind Singh sought to strengthen the community through a shared discipline, clear commitment to Sikh teachings and collective responsibility. At Anandpur Sahib, on the occasion of Baisakhi in 1699, he established the Khalsa, the initiated Sikh order.

Khalsa: The initiated Sikh community organised through a common religious discipline and commitment to the Sikh faith. The Khalsa is an important institution within Sikhism; the term should not be confused with the Guru Granth Sahib, which is the sacred scripture and eternal Guru.

The Panj Pyare

The first 5 initiates of the Khalsa are remembered as the Panj Pyare, meaning the Five Beloved Ones. Their initiation marked the beginning of the formally organised Khalsa order.

The initiation ceremony is associated with Khande di Pahul, in which the initiate formally enters the Khalsa discipline. The initiate receives amrit, prepared by stirring sweetened water with a double-edged sword while sacred hymns are recited. The account of the first initiation also emphasises that membership and religious responsibility were not to be determined by caste background.

The Five Ks of the Khalsa

The Khalsa identity is associated with 5 articles of faith, traditionally called the Five Ks because their names begin with the letter K.

ArticleMeaningWhat to recognise
KeshUncut hairKeeping the hair unshorn as part of religious discipline
KanghaCombA comb used to keep the hair orderly
KaraSteel braceletA circular bracelet worn as an article of faith
KachheraShort breechesA specified form of undergarment
KirpanSword or ceremonial bladeAn article associated with responsibility and the defence of righteousness

These are the Five Ks, not 5 different ceremonies. Each term names an article associated with Khalsa identity.

From Khalsa formation to the eternal Guru

The formation of the Khalsa and the recognition of the Guru Granth Sahib are related but different events.

  • 1699, Anandpur Sahib: Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa and its collective discipline.
  • 1708, Nanded: Before his death, Guru Gobind Singh directed the Sikhs to recognise the Guru Granth Sahib as the continuing spiritual Guru, ending the succession of human Gurus.

The Khalsa provided a distinct initiated identity and shared discipline. The Guru Granth Sahib provided continuing spiritual guidance through the sacred compositions. The two institutions therefore perform different roles within the Sikh tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Guru Gobind Singh: 10th and last human Sikh Guru.
  • Khalsa: established on Baisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur Sahib.
  • Panj Pyare: the first 5 initiates of the Khalsa.
  • Five Ks: Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kachhera and Kirpan.
  • 1708: Guru Granth Sahib recognised as the eternal Guru at Nanded.
  • Trap: The Khalsa was established in 1699; the succession of human Gurus ended in 1708.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chapter Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed p. 118; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, chapter Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, printed p. 164; SGPC, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and Ten Guru Sahibs, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The formation of the Khalsa in 1699 gave the initiated Sikh community a distinct collective discipline.

title: Guru Gobind Singh and the Formation of the Khalsa

body:
What is the Guru Granth Sahib?

The Guru Granth Sahib is the principal sacred scripture of Sikhism and is revered by Sikhs as the eternal Guru. It contains devotional compositions associated with Sikh Gurus and other religious poets. Its authority rests on the teachings preserved in the scripture rather than on the continuation of an individual human Guru.

The text grew through a historical process. Guru Arjan prepared the first major compilation, the Adi Granth, in 1604. The compositions of Guru Tegh Bahadur were incorporated later under Guru Gobind Singh, who conferred Guruship on the sacred text in 1708.

How the scripture developed

Stage 1: The Adi Granth of 1604

Guru Arjan, the 5th Sikh Guru, gathered the compositions of Guru Nanak and the succeeding Gurus, added his own hymns and included selected devotional compositions of other religious figures.

Bhai Gurdas wrote the manuscript as its scribe. The compilation was installed at Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, in 1604, with Baba Buddha serving as its first granthi.

Three different roles: Guru Arjan was the compiler of the 1604 Adi Granth; Bhai Gurdas was its scribe; Baba Buddha was its first granthi. These roles must not be interchanged.

Stage 2: Inclusion of the 9th Guru's compositions

Guru Arjan's original compilation contained the compositions of the first 5 Sikh Gurus. The hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the 9th Guru, entered the later recension associated with Guru Gobind Singh, the 10th Guru.

Thus, 1604 refers to the first compilation by Guru Arjan, while the later form of the scripture incorporates compositions that were not yet present in that original compilation.

Stage 3: The scripture receives Guruship

In 1708, at Nanded, Guru Gobind Singh directed the Sikhs to recognise the Guru Granth Sahib as the continuing Guru. The succession of human Sikh Gurus therefore ended with the 10th Guru, while the spiritual authority of the sacred word continued.

The Adi Granth and the Guru Granth Sahib should not be treated as 2 unrelated scriptures. The former name refers especially to the foundational compilation, and the latter to the sacred scripture in its later authoritative form and its status as Guru.

Who contributed to the Guru Granth Sahib?

The scripture is distinctive because it preserves compositions not only of Sikh Gurus but also of devotional poets from different religious and social backgrounds. Its contents connect the Sikh tradition with the wider devotional culture of medieval India without making all these contributors Sikh Gurus.

The 6 Sikh Gurus represented in the scripture

The standard enumeration identifies the compositions of 6 Sikh Gurus:

  • Guru Nanak, the 1st Guru.
  • Guru Angad, the 2nd Guru.
  • Guru Amar Das, the 3rd Guru.
  • Guru Ram Das, the 4th Guru.
  • Guru Arjan, the 5th Guru.
  • Guru Tegh Bahadur, the 9th Guru.

This means that the Gurus represented in the principal scriptural group are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 9. The number 10 refers to the total line of human Sikh Gurus, not to the number of Gurus whose compositions form this group.

Bhagats and other contributors

A Bhagat is a devotee or devotional poet. The scripture includes compositions attributed to 15 Bhagats. Important examples are:

  • Kabir: A devotional poet associated with belief in one formless God and criticism of empty ritual and caste distinctions.
  • Shaikh Farid or Baba Farid: A Sufi-associated poet whose verses demonstrate the presence of Islamic devotional expression in the scripture.
  • Namdev: A devotional poet associated with the Bhakti tradition of Maharashtra.
  • Ravidas or Raidas: A devotional saint whose teachings emphasised devotion and challenged social inequality.

These figures are contributors whose compositions are preserved in the scripture; they are not counted among the 10 Sikh Gurus. Their presence illustrates the broad devotional range of the Guru Granth Sahib.

The scripture also contains compositions by Bhatt poets, or bards, and other Sikh devotees. A common introductory enumeration identifies 36 contributors, grouped as 6 Sikh Gurus, 15 Bhagats, 11 Bhatts and 4 other Sikh contributors. This is a classification of contributors, not a division into 36 chapters.

Language, script and musical arrangement

The Guru Granth Sahib is written in the Gurmukhi script. Its compositions reflect Punjabi and other regional linguistic traditions, with vocabulary and poetic influences from several languages. Consequently, the script in which a text is written should not be confused with the spoken language or linguistic form of every composition.

The hymns are organised substantially by ragas, or musical modes used for devotional singing. The standard scripture uses 31 principal ragas. This musical arrangement reflects the importance of shabad kirtan, the singing of sacred hymns, in Sikh religious practice.

The standard printed Guru Granth Sahib contains 1430 angs, conventionally described as pages. The word ang is used for a numbered part or page of the sacred scripture.

Do not confuse the numbers

  • 10: Total number of human Sikh Gurus.
  • 6: Sikh Gurus whose compositions form the standard scriptural contributor group.
  • 15: Bhagats represented in the scripture.
  • 31: Principal ragas used to organise the hymns.
  • 1430: Angs in the standard printed text.

Chronology of the main developments

The development of the Sikh tradition can be followed through a few connected milestones. Guru Nanak was born in 1469 and designated Guru Angad as his successor in 1539. Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604 and was executed in 1606. Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa in 1699 and conferred Guruship on the Guru Granth Sahib in 1708.

These dates describe different kinds of events: the birth and succession of Gurus, compilation of a sacred text, a major martyrdom, formation of an initiated community and transfer of spiritual authority to scripture. Distinguishing the kind of event is as important as remembering its year.

Prelims focus

  • 1604: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth; Bhai Gurdas was the scribe and Baba Buddha the first granthi.
  • 6 Guru contributors: Gurus 1–5 and 9.
  • Kabir, Farid, Namdev and Ravidas: important non-Guru devotional contributors.
  • Gurmukhi: script; raga: musical mode.
  • 31 ragas and 1430 angs in the standard scripture.
  • Trap: Guru Gobind Singh was the 10th Guru, but Guru Arjan compiled the original Adi Granth in 1604.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, chapter Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed pp. 117–118; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, chapter Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, section 8.2, printed pp. 163–164; SGPC, Sri Guru Granth Sahib and Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, consulted 20 November 2026; Gurdwara Sahib Darwin, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji: History, Compilation and Significance, section on contributors, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Guru Granth Sahib: Compilation, Contributors and Sacred Authority
